overview: This card follows Jordan from the atlas’s 1938 opening through the independent Hashemite kingdom. In 1938, it was still Transjordan under British protection; independence came in 1946. The first outline is incomplete, even missing Amman, and later shapes do not track the kingdom’s changing administration of the West Bank. Treat these outlines as approximate display coverage, not a precise historical border or a map of one people. Ancient societies in this region have separate histories.

periods.title: Transjordan before independence
periods.summary: The emirate remained under British protection before the kingdom’s independence declaration in May 1946.

periods.title: A kingdom across changing borders
periods.summary: After the 1948 war, Jordan administered and annexed the West Bank. The constitution and monarchy developed amid regional tensions.

periods.title: War, internal conflict and disengagement
periods.summary: Israel occupied the West Bank in 1967. Fighting within Jordan followed; in 1988 the kingdom severed its legal and administrative ties to the West Bank.

periods.title: A peace treaty with Israel
periods.summary: The 1994 treaty established a framework for peace, recognized boundaries and cooperation over shared water resources.

periods.title: Abdullah II and regional pressures
periods.summary: Abdullah II succeeded Hussein in 1999. A January 2026 assessment describes continuing royal power and close, sometimes difficult regional partnerships.

sections.title: A kingdom, its neighbors and political choices

items.text: Transjordan’s path to independence did not begin with a new map color in 1938. It had developed under British protection after the First World War. On 25 May 1946 it declared independence with Britain’s agreement. US recognition followed in January 1949. Independence, foreign recognition and the atlas’s chosen starting date therefore describe three different things.

Jordan’s amended constitution combines a hereditary monarchy with parliamentary institutions. The king appoints the prime minister and the Senate, while the House of Representatives is elected. This structure gives royal authority a major role in governing, rather than making the monarch only a ceremonial figure.

The 1948 war brought Palestinian refugees and placed the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, under Jordanian administration. Jordan annexed the West Bank in 1950, but the annexation gained little international recognition. Israel occupied it in the 1967 war, and more Palestinians fled eastward. Families’ histories therefore crossed a river that political maps repeatedly treated differently.

In September 1970, a violent struggle erupted between the Jordanian army and Palestinian guerrilla organizations. Known as Black September, it caused extensive suffering and destruction; the armed groups were expelled in 1971. The conflict should not be equated with all Palestinians in Jordan. In 1988, the kingdom ended its legal and administrative ties to the West Bank.

Jordan and Israel signed their peace treaty on 26 October 1994. It addressed borders, security and practical cooperation, including water from shared rivers and groundwater. Peace involved technical work as well as ceremonies: officials had to agree how resources would be allocated and disputes handled. The treaty did not settle all Palestinian claims or end conflict elsewhere in the region.

Abdullah II became king in 1999 after his father Hussein died. Parliament remained part of government, but the king retained broad powers to appoint officials and approve laws. A January 2026 Congressional Research Service assessment also describes Jordan’s close ties to the United States and its role in diplomacy involving Israel, Palestinians and Syria.

Political participation has also faced limits. The Islamic Action Front won 31 of 138 parliamentary seats in 2024. In April 2025, authorities banned the related Muslim Brotherhood organization; a January 2026 assessment distinguished this from the party’s legal position. Those developments illustrate why an election result alone cannot explain how freely political groups can operate.

An extraordinary modern conservation project began with fragile ancient plaster figures recovered at Ain Ghazal near Amman in 1985. Conservators protected the contents of their pit with foil, foam and a wooden crate for laboratory excavation. The group included three two-headed busts. Years of careful work helped preserve these Neolithic objects, which long predate the modern kingdom. Sometimes archaeology means moving the soil before daring to remove the treasure.

At Allan, the SESAME research centre opened in May 2017. Its synchrotron light helps researchers examine materials in exceptional detail, supporting work in fields such as medicine, archaeology and materials science. The centre brought scientists from eight members into one international project, including neighbors with difficult political relationships. Sharing a laboratory offered a practical way to cooperate.

Mansaf is a meal made for sharing. UNESCO’s 2022 description explains how sheep or goat meat cooks in yogurt sauce, then sits with rice or bulgur over thin bread. Relatives carry platters to guests, traditionally with several people gathering around each one. There are enough layers to make a very serious sandwich jealous, although mansaf is eaten as a shared meal rather than a sandwich.

Preparing mansaf can itself be a social occasion, with conversation, stories and singing around the work. Recipes and skills pass between generations, and culinary institutions teach them too. Customs also change: UNESCO notes that some diners now use plates and spoons alongside the tradition of eating with the right hand. A living tradition can have both continuity and room for personal preference.

Article 20 includes “التعليم الأساسي إلزامي للأردنيين”, rendered by the Ministry of Justice as “Elementary education shall be compulsory for Jordanians”. This is Arabic, read from right to left, quoted from the current official text of the 1952 constitution as amended. The article also provides for free government schooling. This modern typed sample illustrates a legal commitment, not proof that every child can attend without difficulty.

Learning support often happens beyond the ordinary classroom. UNICEF’s 2025 results recorded extra Arabic and mathematics help for 20,000 children in 114 Makani centres. Reading-recovery work also reached children in Azraq and Zaatari refugee camps. Such programs respond to real barriers, including poverty, disability and interrupted schooling, rather than assuming that enrollment alone guarantees a child can read confidently.

Jordan’s health system serves both citizens and people displaced from neighboring countries. A WHO and Ministry of Health review published in June 2024 describes subsidized essential services for vulnerable refugees and migrants, alongside continuing delivery challenges. Refugee healthcare and host-community healthcare share staff, facilities and budgets. Subsidized access does not mean that every service is free or equally easy to reach.

Vaccines need a dependable journey from warehouse to clinic. A WHO report from March 2025 describes new storage in Irbid, a solar-powered national vaccine warehouse, additional refrigerators and refrigerated trucks. These improvements supported immunization for refugees and host communities. The cold chain is an invisible part of a vaccination appointment: before the nurse gives a dose, transport and storage teams have already done essential work.

sections.title: Water, toilets and dignity at home

items.text: During preparations to reopen schools in 2020, UNICEF described a greywater system for toilets at Samir Al-Refai School in Amman, alongside drinking-water stations and soap. Reusing suitable wastewater can reduce demand for fresh water. Repairs to handwashing facilities in other schools formed part of the COVID-19 response. A safe school day depends on bathrooms and sinks as well as desks and books.

Water conservation continued in later school projects. UNICEF’s 2025 results list greywater treatment and reuse systems in 35 schools in Irbid and Mafraq, benefiting nearly 40,000 students. Climate Action Clubs also involved children in schools and Makani centres. Jordan’s scarce and sometimes intermittent supplies make caring for water an everyday concern, not merely a topic in a science textbook.

An August 2026 UNICEF account follows Khadija and her seven children in Azraq camp, after their flight from Syria in 2014. They had relied on shared bathrooms with poor lighting. A private household latrine and drainage connection gave the family more privacy and made washing easier for the children. This is one family’s experience, but it shows how a door that locks can change daily life.

ending.text: Jordan continues as a kingdom; this atlas record has no historical end date. Its 2100 geometry cutoff is a display horizon, not a prediction. Dated accounts through 2026 show a state managing regional tensions while families, schools and health services adapt. The political history includes changing borders and institutions, but no single war or royal succession erased the communities living here.
